about.title:
From shaders
to screws
about.lead: I’m a creative technologist from Utrecht. For almost a decade I’ve been chasing the same little moment: when a piece of technology stops feeling like technology and starts feeling like a small magic trick.
body: Most of my work lives somewhere between the screen and the real world. I’ve built things that put virtual objects on streets, turned books into interactive worlds, connected strangers through AR and convinced people to have conversations with fictional characters. I like being close to the entire machine — the pixels, the code, the hardware, the people using it and the weird things that happen when all of those collide.

A lot of what I know came from breaking things on purpose. I like finding technology before it has a comfortable workflow, when the documentation is incomplete and everyone is still figuring out what it can become. ARKit before it had a friendly abstraction layer. Multiplayer AR before the tools were ready. Spatial computing before anyone knew what to call it. The unfinished parts are usually where the interesting questions live.

I have one theory I keep coming back to: the demo is a liar. A prototype on my desk can look like the future, but the real world always gets the final word. Networks disappear, hardware behaves strangely and someone will always use your carefully designed interface in a way you never imagined. That is where the real engineering starts.

Right now I’m connecting VR players without letting them physically connect with each other (which sounds easier than it is), experimenting with new ideas and building things that probably have no business working yet. If you enjoy exploring the edges of what technology can do, we’ll probably have something to talk about.
